# Binary Search as a Tool {#sec-bst} ::: {.callout-note title="Sources"} **CPH** ch. 3 "Sorting" (its binary-search section: the jump formulation, `lower_bound`/`upper_bound`, and finding the smallest solution of a monotone test) · **CP-Algorithms** "Binary search" (the `lo`/`hi` invariant, search on the answer) · **Knuth**, *TAOCP* vol. 3, §6.2.1 (searching an ordered table) · **Bentley**, *Programming Pearls*, column 4 (proving a binary search correct) · **cppreference** on `std::lower_bound`, `std::upper_bound`, `std::equal_range` (the half-open range contract and the partition requirement) · **Python `bisect`** documentation (insertion points, `key=`) · **Problem statements** of the eight problems solved here (LeetCode, Codeforces). Coverage: monotone predicates and the loop invariant, the two library brackets, sort-then-search, search over prefix sums and prefix maxima, and a first search on the answer. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"} - State a **monotone predicate** for a search problem and write the loop that finds its **first true**, with an invariant you can prove: initialisation, both branches, termination (@sec-bst-a1). - Use `bisect_left` / `bisect_right` (C++ `lower_bound` / `upper_bound`) to answer "how many $< x$", "how many $\le x$", "where does the run of $x$ start and end", and "how many in $[L, R]$" with one or two calls (@sec-bst-a2, @sec-bst-p1). - Decide when to **sort once and answer many queries** by binary search, and estimate the break-even number of queries (@sec-bst-a3). - Build a **derived monotone array**, prefix sums of non-negative values or prefix maxima of anything, and binary search it instead of the data (@sec-bst-a4, @sec-bst-p3). - Recognise a **search on the answer**: the unknown is a value in a range with a monotone feasibility test, and you binary search that range, then handle "closest to a target" with a two-candidate seam check (@sec-bst-a5, @sec-bst-p4). ::: ## Why this matters {#sec-bst-why} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Think of looking up a word in a paper dictionary. You never read page by page: you open the middle, see whether your word comes before or after, and throw away half the book. Each look halves what is left, so $n$ pages need only about $\log_2 n$ looks: $20$ looks are enough for a million pages, $30$ for a billion. **Binary search** is that habit made exact. It needs only one thing: a yes/no question whose answers, read from left to right, go *no, no, …, no, yes, yes, …, yes*. The search finds where the first *yes* is. ::: The arrays volume has been building structure that later techniques can spend. @sec-srt showed that a sort buys three things: neighbours, a canonical order to count over, and **monotonicity**. This chapter spends the third. Two pointers (@sec-tp-count) already used monotonicity by *walking*: when a boundary only moves one way, one sweep finds it for every position in $O(n)$ total. Binary search uses it by *jumping*: when you need the boundary for one question at a time, halving finds it in $O(\log n)$ without touching most of the array. And prefix sums (@sec-pref-def) build new arrays that are monotone even when the data is not, which turns "how many items fit under a budget?" into a search. You have met the pieces before. @sec-pf-p1-insert proved a binary search correct with a loop invariant, and @sec-lang-p4 listed the library calls. This chapter turns those into a tool you reach for without thinking, in five lessons: - **A1. The predicate and the window.** Every binary search is a monotone yes/no question plus a window `[lo, hi]` that always contains the first *yes* and halves at every step. - **A2. The two brackets.** `bisect_left` and `bisect_right` (C++ `lower_bound`, `upper_bound`) are A1's loop with the question fixed to "$a[i] \ge x$?" and "$a[i] > x$?". Counts, runs and insertion points are one or two calls. - **A3. Sort, then search.** When the data is fixed and the queries are many, pay $O(n\log n)$ once and answer each query in $O(\log n)$. - **A4. Search a derived array.** Prefix sums of non-negative values and prefix maxima of any values are monotone arrays *you build*; searching them answers budget and threshold questions. - **A5. Search the answer.** When the unknown is a value with a monotone "is this enough?" test, binary search the range of values; no array is searched at all. Four patterns then spend these lessons on eight problems. Everything sharper (rotated arrays, peak finding, ternary search, binary search over real numbers, interactive judges, and search on the answer as a full technique) is the subject of the Binary Search volume later in the book; this chapter is the everyday tool. ## A1. The monotone predicate and the lo/hi invariant {#sec-bst-a1} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Binary search does not really need "the array is sorted". It needs a question $P(i)$ about positions whose answers go **false, false, …, false, true, true, …, true** as $i$ grows; such a question is called **monotone**. A sorted array gives one for free ("is $b[i] \ge x$?"), but so do prefix sums, prefix maxima, and many problems where $i$ is not even an index (A5). The job is to find the **first true**, the flip point. Keep a window $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi}]$ that always contains it; each look at the middle discards the half that cannot. ::: Write the invariant first; the code follows from it. ```text P(i) is monotone on 0..n-1: false ... false TRUE ... true (find the first TRUE) convention: P(n) = true (an imaginary true just past the end, meaning "none") lo, hi = 0, n invariant: the first true lies in [lo, hi] while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 # lo <= mid < hi, so mid is a real index if P(mid): hi = mid # mid could be the first true: keep it else: lo = mid + 1 # mid is false: the first true is right of it answer = lo # lo == hi: the first true, or n if there is none ``` **Why it is correct.** *Initialisation*: the first true is somewhere in $0..n$ (with the convention, $n$ means "none"), so $[0, n]$ contains it. *Maintenance*: if $P(\mathit{mid})$ is true, the first true is at $\mathit{mid}$ or to its left, so $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{mid}]$ still contains it; if false, monotonicity says everything at or left of $\mathit{mid}$ is false, so the first true is in $[\mathit{mid}+1, \mathit{hi}]$. *Termination*: because `mid` rounds down, $\mathit{lo} \le \mathit{mid} < \mathit{hi}$, so both branches strictly shrink the window; when $\mathit{lo} = \mathit{hi}$ the window holds one candidate and that is the answer. The window size goes $n+1 \to \lceil (n+1)/2 \rceil \to \dots$, so the loop runs at most $\lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil$ times. Two classic bugs break exactly one of these steps. Writing `hi = mid - 1` on the true branch can throw away the first true itself (maintenance fails). Writing `lo = mid` on the false branch stops the window from shrinking when $\mathit{hi} = \mathit{lo} + 1$, because then $\mathit{mid} = \mathit{lo}$ and nothing changes: an infinite loop (termination fails). The pair `hi = mid` / `lo = mid + 1` with `while lo < hi` is one consistent contract; the other common one is the closed window `while lo <= hi` with `hi = mid - 1`, shown in the demo below. Pick one and derive every line from its invariant. ::: {#fig-bst-anim-window} ::: {#d20b72f1 .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
probe mid=3: b[mid]=7 vs 6 -> window [0,3]
probe mid=1: b[mid]=3 vs 6 -> window [2,3]
probe mid=2: b[mid]=5 vs 6 -> window [3,3]; lo == hi == 3, the first b[i] >= 6
``` ::: ::: The window $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi}]$ closing on $[1,3,5,7,9,11]$ in search of the first element $\ge 6$. Grey cells are proven to be on the wrong side of the flip and are never looked at again. Three probes reduce the seven candidate answers ($0$ to $6$) to one: index $3$, the value $7$. ::: ::: {#arr-bst-a1-demo .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def first_true(P, n): lo, hi = 0, n # the first true lies in [lo, hi]; n means "none" while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if P(mid): hi = mid else: lo = mid + 1 return lo # first i with P(i) true, else n def first_true_closed(P, n): # the other contract: closed window [lo, hi] lo, hi = 0, n - 1 while lo <= hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if P(mid): hi = mid - 1 # mid is a candidate; remember it lives at hi + 1 else: lo = mid + 1 return lo # lo == hi + 1 == the first true, or n def last_true(P, n): # P is true ... true false ... false return first_true(lambda i: not P(i), n) - 1 # -1 means "no true at all" b = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11] assert first_true(lambda i: b[i] >= 6, len(b)) == 3 assert first_true(lambda i: b[i] >= 1, len(b)) == 0 # flip at the very front assert first_true(lambda i: b[i] >= 100, len(b)) == len(b) # no true: returns n assert last_true(lambda i: b[i] <= 6, len(b)) == 2 # the last element <= 6 is b[2] = 5 for _ in range(500): arr = sorted(random.randint(0, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 12))) t = random.randint(-2, 55) P = lambda i: arr[i] >= t assert first_true(P, len(arr)) == first_true_closed(P, len(arr)) == bisect.bisect_left(arr, t) assert last_true(lambda i: arr[i] <= t, len(arr)) == bisect.bisect_right(arr, t) - 1 probes = 0 def counting_P(i): global probes probes += 1 return i >= 123_457 assert first_true(counting_P, 10**6) == 123_457 and probes <= math.ceil(math.log2(10**6 + 1)) print("a1 demo OK, probes on n = 10^6:", probes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a1 demo OK, probes on n = 10^6: 20 ``` ::: ::: Three things in the demo are worth reading slowly. First, `first_true` never calls `P(n)`: since `mid < hi <= n`, the imaginary true past the end is never evaluated, which is why the convention costs nothing. Second, the closed-window version returns the same index: both are correct, they just keep different invariants (the closed one keeps "the first true is in $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi}+1]$"). Third, "the **last** true of a true…false predicate" needs no new loop: it is one before the first true of the opposite predicate. On a sorted array that is "the last element $\le x$" $=$ `bisect_right(a, x) - 1`, with $-1$ meaning "none". **The sibling solved in @sec-pf-p1-insert.** Search Insert Position is this loop with $P(i) = [\mathit{nums}[i] \ge \mathit{target}]$, proved correct there step by step as the first example of a loop invariant. ::: {.problem-card} [Problem]{.card-kicker} **Search insert position** [LC 35 · Search Insert Position](https://leetcode.com/problems/search-insert-position/){difficulty="Easy"} Both cases ask for the same thing: the first index $p$ with $a_p \ge x$ (the **lower bound**). Keep a half-open window $[lo, hi)$ that is known to contain this boundary, and halve it. [Solved in full in @sec-pf-p1-insert.]{.card-link} ::: ## A2. `lower_bound` and `upper_bound`: counting is two probes {#sec-bst-a2} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} In real code you rarely write A1's loop; you call one of two library functions. **`bisect_left(a, x)`** (C++ `lower_bound`) is the first index with $a[i] \ge x$; **`bisect_right(a, x)`** (C++ `upper_bound`) is the first index with $a[i] > x$. Both assume `a` is sorted. Picture two doors around the block of $x$'s: the left door has everything $< x$ before it, the right door everything $\le x$ before it. Every counting question about a sorted array is read off those two doors. ::: The four readings, each one A1's `first_true` with a fixed predicate: ```text bisect_left(a, x) first i with a[i] >= x = #elements < x = insertion point before equal values bisect_right(a, x) first i with a[i] > x = #elements <= x = insertion point after equal values run of x [bisect_left, bisect_right) count(x) = right - left (0 if x is absent) #elements in [L, R] bisect_right(a, R) - bisect_left(a, L) last element <= x a[bisect_right(a, x) - 1] if bisect_right(a, x) > 0 first element >= x a[bisect_left(a, x)] if bisect_left(a, x) < n ``` C++ returns iterators: subtract `begin()` to get the index, and `equal_range(first, last, x)` returns both brackets at once. Both languages also accept an ordering: Python 3.10+ has `bisect_left(a, x, key=f)`, and C++ takes a comparator, which is how you search a descending array (@sec-bst-p2-b). On a `std::set`, call the member `s.lower_bound(x)`; the free function on set iterators is linear (@sec-lang-p4). ::: {#fig-bst-a2-brackets} ::: {#arr-bst-a2-fig .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](011_binary_search_files/figure-html/arr-bst-a2-fig-output-1.png){#arr-bst-a2-fig-1 width=462 height=182} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](011_binary_search_files/figure-html/arr-bst-a2-fig-output-2.png){#arr-bst-a2-fig-2 width=462 height=182} ::: ::: On $[1,2,2,2,3,5]$ with $x = 2$: `bisect_left` stops at the run's left door (index $1$; everything before it is $< 2$), `bisect_right` at its right door (index $4$; everything before it is $\le 2$). The three $2$'s sit between them, so `count(2) = 4 - 1 = 3`, `#(<2) = 1` and `#(<=2) = 4`. Most off-by-one bugs in counting problems are a `_left`/`_right` mix-up; draw the two doors and the right call follows. ::: ::: {#arr-bst-a2-demo .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} a = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 5] assert bisect.bisect_left(a, 2) == 1 and bisect.bisect_right(a, 2) == 4 assert bisect.bisect_right(a, 2) - bisect.bisect_left(a, 2) == 3 # count of 2 assert bisect.bisect_left(a, 2) == sum(1 for x in a if x < 2) # count < 2 assert bisect.bisect_right(a, 2) == sum(1 for x in a if x <= 2) # count <= 2 assert bisect.bisect_right(a, 4) - bisect.bisect_left(a, 2) == sum(1 for x in a if 2 <= x <= 4) assert bisect.bisect_left(a, 4) == bisect.bisect_right(a, 4) == 5 # absent: empty run assert a[bisect.bisect_right(a, 4) - 1] == 3 # last element <= 4 for _ in range(300): # every reading, at random s = sorted(random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10))) L, R = sorted(random.randint(-1, 10) for _ in range(2)) assert bisect.bisect_right(s, R) - bisect.bisect_left(s, L) == sum(L <= v <= R for v in s) k = bisect.bisect_right(s, R) assert (s[k - 1] if k else None) == max((v for v in s if v <= R), default=None) print("a2 demo OK") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a2 demo OK ``` ::: ::: The absent-value line is the one people distrust. For $4$, which is not in `a`, both brackets land on index $5$: the run is empty and `right - left = 0`. The count formula needs no special case for "not present", and neither do the problems that use it: @sec-bst-p1-a counts negatives as `bisect_left(nums, 0)` even when there are none, and @sec-bst-p1-b lists the run `range(bisect_left, bisect_right)` even when it is empty. ## A3. Sort, then search: pay once, query many {#sec-bst-a3} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} If the data does not change but you must answer **many** "find / count / nearest" questions about it, sort it once. The sort costs $O(n\log n)$; after that each question is a binary search, $O(\log n)$, instead of a scan, $O(n)$. Often the question only becomes monotone *after* sorting: "how many prices are $\le m$?" has no structure in a shuffled list and is one `bisect_right` in a sorted one. ::: The three steps: ```text 1. sort the data (or build a derived monotone array from it) O(n log n), once 2. phrase each query as a monotone predicate on the sorted order 3. answer it with bisect_left / bisect_right O(log n) per query ``` **When it pays.** Answering $q$ queries by scanning costs about $q \cdot n$. Sorting first costs about $n\log_2 n + q\log_2 n$. The sort wins once $q$ is larger than roughly $\log_2 n$ queries (constant factors aside): for $n = 10^5$ that is a few dozen queries, and with $q = 10^5$ queries the difference is $10^{10}$ against a few million operations. For a single query, scanning is cheaper than sorting. When the data **changes** between queries (insertions and deletions), a sorted list costs $O(n)$ per insertion; use an ordered container (C++ `std::set` / `multiset`, @sec-lang-p4) or the tree structures of later volumes. When all the queries are known in advance, a third option is to sort the queries too and sweep both sorted lists with two pointers: two sorts, then a linear walk. ::: {#fig-bst-a3-multi} ::: {#arr-bst-a3-fig .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](011_binary_search_files/figure-html/arr-bst-a3-fig-output-1.png){#arr-bst-a3-fig-1 width=548 height=318} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](011_binary_search_files/figure-html/arr-bst-a3-fig-output-2.png){#arr-bst-a3-fig-2 width=548 height=318} ::: ::: $[40,10,30,50,20]$ sorted to $[10,20,30,40,50]$; the queries $15, 30, 45$ land at insertion points $1, 2, 4$ with one binary search each. The sort is a fixed cost; its value grows with the number of queries. ::: ::: {#arr-bst-a3-demo .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} data = [40, 10, 30, 50, 20] s = sorted(data) # pay once def count_le(x): # many cheap queries return bisect.bisect_right(s, x) def first_ge(x): # smallest value >= x, or None i = bisect.bisect_left(s, x) return s[i] if i < len(s) else None def nearest(x): # closest value; ties to the smaller i = bisect.bisect_left(s, x) cands = [s[j] for j in (i - 1, i) if 0 <= j < len(s)] return min(cands, key=lambda v: (abs(v - x), v)) assert count_le(15) == 1 and count_le(30) == 3 and count_le(100) == 5 assert first_ge(25) == 30 and first_ge(50) == 50 and first_ge(51) is None assert nearest(34) == 30 and nearest(35) == 30 and nearest(36) == 40 and nearest(-7) == 10 for _ in range(300): x = random.randint(0, 60) assert count_le(x) == sum(v <= x for v in data) assert nearest(x) == min(data, key=lambda v: (abs(v - x), v)) print("a3 demo OK") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a3 demo OK ``` ::: ::: `nearest` is the move behind every "closest value" question: in a sorted array, the closest value to $x$ is one of the two neighbours of its insertion point, `s[i - 1]` and `s[i]`, so one search plus two comparisons replaces a scan. @sec-bst-p2 builds on exactly this. **The sibling solved in @sec-lang-p4-drink.** Interesting Drink is A3 in its purest form: sort the prices once, and each day's budget $m$ is answered by `bisect_right(prices, m)`. ::: {.problem-card} [Problem]{.card-kicker} **Interesting drink** [CF 706B · Interesting drink](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/706/B){rating="1100"} After sorting the prices, the affordable shops form a prefix, and its length is the number of prices $\le m$: `bisect_right(prices, m)`. [Solved in full in @sec-lang-p4-drink.]{.card-link} ::: ## A4. Searching a derived array: prefix sums and prefix maxima {#sec-bst-a4} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Binary search needs a monotone *sequence*, and some of the most useful ones are sequences **you build**. If every value is non-negative, the running totals (prefix sums) never go down, so "how many items, taken in order, fit in budget $B$?" is one search on the totals. For *any* values, the running maximum (prefix maxima) never goes down either, because a maximum can only grow as you look at more elements. Neither needs the original array to be sorted. ::: Both arrays come from @sec-pref-def and @sec-pref-other; here they are search targets. With `pref[i]` the sum and `pm[i]` the maximum of the first $i + 1$ elements (0-based, inclusive): ```text pref = list(accumulate(a)) non-decreasing only if every a[i] >= 0 #prefixes with total <= B -> bisect_right(pref, B) (items that fit, in order) #items to reach total >= X -> bisect_left(pref, X) + 1 (or "impossible" if == n) pm = list(accumulate(a, max)) non-decreasing for ANY a, no sort needed #prefixes whose max <= K -> bisect_right(pm, K) (longest prefix of elements <= K) ``` ::: {#fig-bst-a4-derive} ::: {#arr-bst-a4-fig .cell renderings='["light","dark"]' execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](011_binary_search_files/figure-html/arr-bst-a4-fig-output-1.png){#arr-bst-a4-fig-1 width=608 height=512} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](011_binary_search_files/figure-html/arr-bst-a4-fig-output-2.png){#arr-bst-a4-fig-2 width=608 height=512} ::: ::: Two derived arrays, both non-decreasing. Top: $[4,3,3,1,1]$ has prefix sums $[4,7,10,11,12]$; with budget $9$, `bisect_right(pref, 9) = 2`, so the first two items fit ($4 + 3 = 7$) and the third busts it ($10$). Bottom: the unsorted $[1,4,2,5,3]$ has prefix maxima $[1,4,4,5,5]$; with limit $4$, `bisect_right(pm, 4) = 3`, so the longest prefix with every element $\le 4$ has length $3$. ::: ::: {#arr-bst-a4-demo .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} a = [4, 3, 3, 1, 1] pref = list(itertools.accumulate(a)) # monotone since a[i] >= 0 assert pref == [4, 7, 10, 11, 12] assert bisect.bisect_right(pref, 9) == 2 # two items fit in budget 9 assert bisect.bisect_left(pref, 11) + 1 == 4 # four items to reach 11 b = [1, 4, 2, 5, 3] pm = list(itertools.accumulate(b, max)) # monotone for ANY b assert pm == [1, 4, 4, 5, 5] assert bisect.bisect_right(pm, 4) == 3 # longest prefix with all <= 4 neg = [3, -2, 4] # a negative value breaks prefix sums pneg = list(itertools.accumulate(neg)) # [3, 1, 5]: not sorted assert pneg == [3, 1, 5] and bisect.bisect_right(pneg, 2) == 2 # claims 2 prefixes are <= 2... assert sum(1 for v in pneg if v <= 2) == 1 # ...but only [3, -2] (sum 1) is for _ in range(300): v = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))] B = random.randint(0, 50) pv = list(itertools.accumulate(v)) assert bisect.bisect_right(pv, B) == sum(1 for t in pv if t <= B) w = [random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))] K = random.randint(-9, 9) longest = next((i for i, x in enumerate(w) if x > K), len(w)) assert bisect.bisect_right(list(itertools.accumulate(w, max)), K) == longest print("a4 demo OK") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a4 demo OK ``` ::: ::: The demo draws the line that matters. `pref` is monotone only *because* the values are non-negative: with $[3, -2, 4]$ the running totals are $[3, 1, 5]$, and `bisect_right` gives a wrong count. (The same negative values break the sliding window in @sec-sw-a5, for the same reason.) Prefix maxima are monotone *unconditionally*, which is why @sec-bst-p3-b searches them on unsorted input. ## A5. A first search on the answer {#sec-bst-a5} ::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"} Until now the thing being searched was an array. Now turn the question around: the unknown is a **number** $v$, say a capacity or a limit, in some range $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi}]$, and you can **check** any guess: "is capacity $v$ enough?". If a bigger $v$ is never worse (once enough, always enough), the answers to the check go no, …, no, yes, …, yes as $v$ grows. That is A1's monotone predicate with $v$ in place of an index, so the same loop finds the smallest $v$ that is enough. No array is searched; the *range of possible answers* is. ::: The template is A1's loop with `a[mid] >= x` replaced by a feasibility check: ```text lo, hi = smallest possible answer, a value known to be feasible while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if feasible(mid): hi = mid # mid is enough: the smallest enough is mid or left else: lo = mid + 1 # mid is not enough: neither is anything smaller answer = lo # for "closest to a target", also compare lo - 1 (@sec-bst-p4-b) ``` The work is in two claims you must check for each problem. **Monotone**: if $v$ is feasible, so is $v + 1$. **Bracketed**: `hi` is feasible (or is the sentinel "none"), and nothing below `lo` can be the answer. The running time is $O(\log(\mathit{hi} - \mathit{lo}))$ checks, times the cost of one check. The standard first example is shipping packages: weights $w_1, \dots, w_n$ must ship **in order** within $D$ days, each day's load at most the ship's capacity $c$; find the smallest $c$ (LC 1011, "Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days"). The check "can capacity $c$ do it in $D$ days?" is a greedy pass: fill each day until the next package would overflow it, and count days. A larger ship never needs more days, so the check is monotone; $c = \max(w)$ is the smallest capacity that can lift every package, and $c = \sum w$ ships everything in one day, so the answer lies in $[\max(w), \sum w]$. ::: {#fig-bst-anim-answer} ::: {#a4612a9a .cell execution_count=10} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
capacity 10 needs 2 days -> hi moves; window [4,10]
capacity 7 needs 3 days -> hi moves; window [4,7]
capacity 5 needs 4 days -> lo moves; window [6,7]
capacity 6 needs 3 days -> hi moves; window [6,6]; the smallest capacity is 6
``` ::: ::: Searching the ship capacity for weights $[3,2,2,4,1,4]$ and $D = 3$ days. The cells are capacities $4..16$, not array positions. Each probe runs the greedy day count once: capacities $10$ and $7$ are enough, $5$ is not, $6$ is. P2 asks for **positions** near a value instead of counts: the closest elements, the farthest valid partner. P3 searches an array that is not the input at all but **built from it**: prefix sums and prefix maxima. P4 drops the array and searches the **answer's own range**. **Recognise it.** The input is sorted (or may be sorted), and the question is "how many $< x$ / $\le x$ / $= x$ / in $[L,R]$", "which indices hold $x$", or "how big are the blocks on each side of a threshold". Two `bisect_left` probes find both positions in $O(\log n)$, with no scan. ::: ::: {.p-approach} 1. **Count both signs directly.** One pass, two counters: `neg += x < 0`, `pos += x > 0`. $O(n)$. 2. **Count the runs.** The negatives are exactly the elements *before the first* $\ge 0$; the positives are exactly the elements *from the first* $\ge 1$ onward. For $[3, 1, 5]$, `pm = [3, 3, 5]` and $B = 2$ gives index $0$ (@sec-bst-a4). ::: **12. [M] Change Eating Queries (@sec-bst-p3-a): for each query $x$, print the **largest** number of candies whose total sugar is **at most** $x$. What changes?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} To fit the most candies under a budget, eat the *smallest* first, so sort **ascending**. Its prefix sums are non-decreasing, and the answer is the number of prefixes with total $\le x$: `bisect_right(pref, x)`. Both the sort direction and the bracket flip: "fewest to reach" uses descending order and `bisect_left`, "most within" uses ascending order and `bisect_right`. The exchange argument is the mirror image: replacing a chosen candy by a smaller unchosen one never raises the total. This is LC 2389 in the practice ladder. ::: **13. [H] @sec-bst-p4-b searches $[0, \max]$ for the first cap $v$ with $S(v) \ge \text{target}$, then compares $v - 1$ and $v$. Prove that the smallest optimal cap is one of these two.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} $S$ is non-decreasing. For $c \ge v$: $S(c) \ge S(v) \ge \text{target}$, so $|S(c) - \text{target}| = S(c) - \text{target} \ge S(v) - \text{target}$; no larger cap beats $v$, and a larger cap that ties loses the tie-break to $v$. For $c \le v - 2$: since $v \le \max(\mathit{arr})$, every cap $c < v - 1$ has at least one element above it, so $S(c + 1) - S(c) \ge 1$ and $S(c) < S(v-1) < \text{target}$; thus $|S(c) - \text{target}| > \text{target} - S(v-1)$, and every smaller cap is strictly worse than $v - 1$. So the smallest optimal cap is $v - 1$ or $v$, and comparing them with ties to $v - 1$ returns it. (If even $S(\max) < \text{target}$, the search ends at $v = \max$ and the same argument applies to the left side.) (@sec-bst-p4-b) ::: **14. [H] For @sec-bst-p4-b, find a case where the answer is not a value of `arr`, and explain why trying only `sorted(set(arr))` fails.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} `arr = [17, 26, 10, 28, 1, 5], target = 17`: $S(3) = 1 + 3 \cdot 5 = 16$ (distance $1$) and $S(4) = 1 + 4 \cdot 5 = 21$ (distance $4$); the answer is $3$, which is not in `arr`. Between two consecutive array values $S$ is linear, rising by the number of elements above the cap per unit, so the closest point to a target can be anywhere inside such a stretch. Trying only the array's values ($1, 5, 10, \dots$) gives $S(1) = 6$ and $S(5) = 1 + 25 = 26$, both worse. Only a search over every integer cap finds $3$ (@sec-bst-p4-b). ::: **15. [H] Compute $\lfloor \sqrt{N} \rfloor$ for $0 \le N \le 10^{18}$ by binary search on the answer, in C++ without overflow.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} The answer is the last $r$ with $r^2 \le N$; the test "$r^2 \le N$" is true…false over $r \in [0, 10^9]$ ($10^9$ squared is exactly $10^{18}$). Search `lo = 0, hi = 1000000000` with the last-true loop of exercise 8 (`mid = lo + (hi - lo + 1) / 2`). Test without overflow: `mid <= N / mid` for `mid > 0` (integer division: $\mathit{mid} \le \lfloor N/\mathit{mid} \rfloor \iff \mathit{mid}^2 \le N$), or compute `mid * mid` in `unsigned long long` or `__int128`; `mid * mid` in `long long` is safe here only because `mid` $\le 10^9$. Floating-point `sqrt` can be off by one near $10^{18}$, which is why the integer search is the safe answer (@sec-bst-a5). ::: **16. [H] Prove that the predicate of @sec-bst-p2-a, $P(l)$: "$x - a[l] \le a[l+k] - x$", is false…true over $l \in [0, n-k-1]$, and that its first true (or $n - k$) is an optimal window start.** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} Let $f(l) = (x - a[l]) - (a[l+k] - x)$. As $l$ grows, $a[l]$ and $a[l+k]$ do not decrease, so $f$ does not increase, and $P(l) = [f(l) \le 0]$ is false…true. Window $l + 1$ differs from window $l$ by dropping $a[l]$ and adding $a[l+k]$. If $P(l)$ is false, $a[l+k]$ is strictly closer than $a[l]$ (the midpoint argument of @sec-bst-p2-a), so window $l + 1$ is better than window $l$. If $P(l)$ is true, $a[l]$ is at least as close (and smaller on a tie), so window $l$ is at least as good as window $l + 1$. Hence the window quality improves strictly up to the first true $l^*$ and never improves after it, and $l^*$ is optimal; if $P$ is never true, the last start $n - k$ is (@sec-bst-p2-a). ::: **17. [H] Special Array with $n = 10^5$ and values up to $10^9$: give an $O(n \log n)$ algorithm, and explain why the answer, if it exists, is found at the flip of "$c(x) \le x$".** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"} Sort once, $c(x) = n - \mathtt{bisect\_left}(s, x)$, and search $x \in [0, n]$ for the first $x$ with $c(x) \le x$; answer it if $c(x) = x$, else $-1$. Total $O(n\log n + \log^2 n)$. The values may be huge but $x$ is a count, so $x \le n$. Correctness: $d(x) = c(x) - x$ strictly decreases (each step raises $x$ by one and $c$ cannot rise), so $d(x) \le 0$ first happens at a single $x^*$; if $d(x) = 0$ anywhere, it is at $x^*$, because before $x^*$ the difference is positive and after it negative (@sec-bst-p4-a). ::: ## Interview questions **1. How do you find the first position where a sorted array is $\ge x$ in $O(\log n)$, and what is the loop invariant?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} `lo, hi = 0, n; while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if a[mid] >= x: hi = mid else: lo = mid + 1; return lo`. Invariant: the first index with $a[i] \ge x$ (or $n$ if none) lies in $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi}]$. Each branch keeps it and shrinks the window, because $\mathit{lo} \le \mathit{mid} < \mathit{hi}$; at `lo == hi` that index is the answer. This is `bisect_left` / `lower_bound` (@sec-bst-a1). ::: **2. How do you count the elements of a sorted array in a closed value range $[L, R]$ with two calls?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} `bisect_right(a, R) - bisect_left(a, L)`. The first term counts the elements $\le R$, the second those $< L$; the difference is the number with $L \le x \le R$. Both calls are $O(\log n)$, and an empty range correctly gives $0$ (@sec-bst-a2). ::: **3. With $q$ queries on $n$ fixed items, when is sorting and binary searching worth it compared with scanning?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Scanning costs about $qn$; sorting first costs about $n\log n + q\log n$. Sorting wins once $q$ exceeds roughly $\log_2 n$ queries, ignoring constants; for one query, scanning is cheaper. If the data changes between queries, a sorted list costs $O(n)$ per insertion, so use an ordered container such as C++ `std::set`. If all queries are known in advance, you can also sort the queries and sweep (@sec-bst-a3). ::: **4. Many queries ask how many items, taken in order, fit in a budget, and you may not reorder them. What do you search?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} The prefix-sum array, if the values are non-negative: it is non-decreasing, and the answer is `bisect_right(pref, budget)`. If values can be negative, prefix sums are not monotone and the search is wrong. If the question is about a maximum ("every item $\le k$") rather than a sum, search the prefix maxima, which are monotone for any input (@sec-bst-a4, @sec-bst-p3). ::: **5. What is "binary search on the answer", and what two things must you prove before using it?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} The unknown is a value in a range $[\mathit{lo}, \mathit{hi}]$ with a check "is $v$ good enough?"; you binary search the range of values, running the check at each probe. You must prove the check is **monotone** (if $v$ passes, so does every larger $v$, or every smaller one) and that the range **brackets** the answer (`hi` passes, nothing below `lo` can be the answer). Example: the smallest ship capacity that delivers packages within $D$ days, searched over $[\max w, \sum w]$ with a greedy day count as the check (@sec-bst-a5). ::: **6. In a "closest to a target" search on the answer, why is the value returned by the search not enough, and what do you compare?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} The search returns the first value whose objective reaches the target. The objective jumps over the target between that value and the one just below it, so the closest value is one of these two; every value further left is further below the target and every value further right further above. Compare both distances and, on a tie, return the smaller value (LC 1300's rule) (@sec-bst-p4-b). ::: **7. Your binary search sometimes loops forever or returns the wrong index. What are the two standard contracts, and which mixtures break?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Half-open: `while lo < hi`, `hi = mid`, `lo = mid + 1`, answer `lo`. Closed: `while lo <= hi`, `hi = mid - 1`, `lo = mid + 1`, answer `lo` (the first true is $\mathit{hi} + 1$ at the end). Mixing them breaks: `while lo <= hi` with `hi = mid` never terminates once `lo == hi`; `while lo < hi` with `hi = mid - 1` can discard the answer; `lo = mid` with a rounding-down `mid` stalls when `hi = lo + 1` (@sec-bst-a1). ::: **8. How do you binary search a non-increasing array, for example to find the first index with `b[j] < v`?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} "`b[j] >= v`" holds on a prefix of a non-increasing array, so the answer is the first index where it fails. Either search a negated copy, `bisect_right([-x for x in b], -v)`, or pass a comparator in C++: `lower_bound(b.begin(), b.end(), v, [](int e, int v) { return e >= v; })`, or `upper_bound(b.begin(), b.end(), v, greater())`. What these functions really require is that the comparator be true on a prefix of the range and false after it (@sec-bst-p2-b). ::: **9. Why do C++ binary searches write `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` instead of `(lo + hi) / 2`?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} `lo + hi` can exceed the largest `int` (about $2.1 \cdot 10^9$) when the search range is large, for example a search on the answer over $[0, 2 \cdot 10^9]$ or indices of a very large array; signed overflow is undefined behaviour. `hi - lo` never overflows when both are in range, so `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` is safe. Joshua Bloch's well-known 2006 note describes exactly this bug in widely used library code. In Python, integers do not overflow (@sec-arr-cost). ::: **10. Does binary search require a sorted array?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} No. It requires a predicate that is false…false true…true over an ordered set of candidates. A sorted array supplies one ("$a[i] \ge x$"), but so do prefix maxima of an unsorted array (Scuza), prefix sums of non-negative values, and ranges of answers with a monotone check (ship capacity, Special Array). Conversely, a sorted array with the wrong predicate (one that flips twice) cannot be binary searched (@sec-bst-a1, @sec-bst-p3-b). ::: **11. How do you find the largest element $\le x$ in a sorted array, and how do you report that none exists?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} `i = bisect_right(a, x)` counts the elements $\le x$; if `i == 0` there is none, otherwise the answer is `a[i - 1]`. In C++: `auto it = upper_bound(a.begin(), a.end(), x);` then `it == a.begin()` means none, else the answer is `*prev(it)`. The smallest element $\ge x$ is the mirror: `a[bisect_left(a, x)]` if that index is $< n$ (@sec-bst-a2). ::: **12. What is the complexity of `std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` on a `std::set`, and what should you call instead?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} It performs $O(\log n)$ comparisons, but set iterators are not random-access, so each jump to the middle walks the tree step by step and the total is $O(n)$. Call the member function `s.lower_bound(x)`, which descends the tree in $O(\log n)$ (@sec-lang-p4). ::: **13. Why can no comparison-based search of a sorted array beat about $\log_2 n$ comparisons in the worst case?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} A search must distinguish $n + 1$ possible outcomes (the insertion point can be any of $0..n$). Each comparison has two outcomes, so after $t$ comparisons at most $2^t$ cases can be told apart; we need $2^t \ge n + 1$, so $t \ge \lceil \log_2(n+1) \rceil$. Binary search meets this bound, so it is optimal among comparison-based methods (the decision-tree argument of @sec-pf-lower-bounds). ::: **14. Is binary search always faster than a linear scan in practice?** ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"} Not always. For very small arrays a linear scan is often as fast or faster, because it reads memory sequentially and its branches are predictable, while binary search jumps around the array. For a single query on unsorted data, scanning ($O(n)$) beats sorting first ($O(n\log n)$). Binary search wins clearly when $n$ is large and the data is already sorted, or when many queries share one sort (@sec-bst-a3). ::: ## Summary ::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"} - **First true:** `lo, hi = 0, n; while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if P(mid): hi = mid else: lo = mid + 1; return lo` ($n$ means none). Last true of the opposite shape: first true of `not P`, minus one (@sec-bst-a1). - **Two brackets:** `bisect_left(a, x)` $=$ #(< x), `bisect_right(a, x)` $=$ #(<= x); run of $x$ $=$ `[left, right)`; count in $[L, R]$ $=$ `right(R) - left(L)`; floor $=$ `a[right(x) - 1]` (@sec-bst-a2, @sec-bst-p1). - **Sort once, query many:** $O(n\log n) + O(\log n)$ per query; nearest value $=$ one of the two neighbours of the insertion point (@sec-bst-a3, @sec-bst-p2). - **Derived monotone array:** prefix sums (values $\ge 0$) or `accumulate(a, max)` (any values); fewest to reach $X$ $=$ `bisect_left(pref, X) + 1`, longest prefix all $\le K$ $=$ `bisect_right(pm, K)` (@sec-bst-a4, @sec-bst-p3). - **Search on the answer:** binary search the value range with a monotone check, `hi` feasible; exact objective: verify at the flip; closest objective: compare `lo - 1` and `lo`, ties to the smaller (@sec-bst-a5, @sec-bst-p4). ::: - Binary search is one loop over a window that always contains the first *yes* of a monotone question; correctness is initialisation, both branches, and a window that strictly shrinks (@sec-bst-a1). - The two library brackets are that loop with the question fixed; every count, run, floor and ceiling on a sorted array is one or two of them, and `_left`/`_right` confusion is the classic off-by-one (@sec-bst-a2, @sec-bst-p1). - Sorting pays for itself once the queries outnumber roughly $\log_2 n$; when data changes between queries, use an ordered container instead (@sec-bst-a3). - "Closest value" questions reduce to the neighbours of an insertion point; "closest $k$" reduces to searching a window start by comparing its two ends (@sec-bst-p2). - On descending data, flip the comparison: negate a copy or pass a comparator that is true on a prefix (@sec-bst-p2-b). - You can manufacture the monotone array: prefix sums need non-negative values, prefix maxima need nothing at all (@sec-bst-a4, @sec-bst-p3). -
